sections.h2: How is Nevada laid out for people selling a house?
sections.html:
Nevada has 16 counties and one independent city, Carson City, and almost all of the people live in two of them. The Census Bureau puts the state at 3,282,188 residents on July 1, 2025, with Clark County at 2,407,226 and Washoe County at 509,386. Clark alone is roughly 73 percent of the state total, by simple division of those two figures.

The rest of the map is large and thinly settled. The Census Bureau lists Nevada's land area at 109,860.46 square miles and its 2020 density at 28.3 people per square mile. A seller in a rural county and a seller in the Las Vegas valley deal with the same state statutes, but with very different local offices, buyer pools and travel distances.

sections.h2: Who sends the property tax bill in Nevada?
sections.html:
Your county bills locally assessed property tax, and the county assessor or treasurer is the office to call about a bill. The Nevada Department of Taxation explains that locally assessed tax covers residential homes, commercial buildings and land, and that each county sets its rate within a state cap.

The installment dates are set in NRS 361.483. A taxpayer who chooses to pay in installments owes the first on the third Monday of August, the second on the first Monday of October, the third on the first Monday of January and the fourth on the first Monday of March. Late payments can bring penalties and interest.

Two features matter to sellers more than most people expect:

  • The 3 percent cap. Under NRS 361.4723, the tax bill on an owner's primary residence is capped through a partial abatement. The Clark County Assessor says only one property in the whole state can be chosen as a primary residence.
  • The cap for everything else. The same Assessor page says a cap of up to 8 percent applies to homes that are not owner occupied, land and commercial buildings, and that new construction gets no cap in its first year.

The Clark County Assessor also warns that any recorded ownership document removes the owner-occupied 3 percent abatement until the new owner returns the postcard the office mails after July 1. A buyer who plans to live in the house should expect that paperwork. Other counties may run the process differently, so check with the assessor where the house sits.

sections.h2: How do appeals and exemptions work?
sections.html:
An owner who disagrees with an assessment files a petition with the County Board of Equalization, usually in January. The Department of Taxation describes the steps as a petition, a review with a possible hearing, and a decision. Pull the Department's appeals page and your county's own calendar before relying on a date.

Nevada also offers exemptions that lower taxable value. The Department lists exemptions for veterans and surviving spouses and a senior citizen tax assistance program, and says you apply through the county assessor's office. Several are claimed by affidavit and renewed on a schedule, so a seller who inherits a house cannot assume the prior owner's exemption carries forward.

For a seller, the practical point is simple. Tax is a lien on the property, and the escrow company will ask the county for the current balance. Ask for that figure early, especially if the last installments are unpaid.

sections.h2: What are the state transfer tax and recording rules?
sections.html:
The Real Property Transfer Tax is collected by the county recorder when the deed is recorded, and the base rate is $1.95 for every $500 of value. The Nevada Department of Taxation adds that Washoe and Churchill Counties charge an extra $0.10 and Clark County an extra $0.60 on top of the base rate.

Each deed presented for recording must come with a Declaration of Value on the form prescribed by the Nevada Tax Commission, under NRS 375. The recorder reviews any claimed exemption. The Department lists 14 exemptions in NRS 375.090, and the list includes a transfer to a family member within the first degree, a transfer between former spouses under a divorce decree, and a deed that takes effect on the grantor's death under NRS 111.109.

sections.h2: What must a Nevada seller disclose?
sections.html:
A seller of residential property must complete a disclosure form and serve it on the buyer at least 10 days before conveyance. That rule is in NRS 113.130, and the form is the one the Real Estate Division approves.

If the seller learns of a new defect, or finds that a disclosed defect has worsened, the buyer must be told in writing no later than conveyance. When the seller will not repair it, the buyer may rescind or close and accept the defect. Rescission has to be in writing, notarized and served within 4 working days after the buyer learns of the defect.

The statute carves out several kinds of sale. They include a foreclosure sale under chapter 107, sales between co-owners, spouses or close relatives, the first sale of a house built by a licensed contractor, and a sale by a fiduciary such as a personal representative, guardian, trustee or agent under a power of attorney who holds title only to arrange the sale for a person who is deceased or incapacitated. A seller may not make a buyer waive the requirement as a condition of sale.

sections.h2: How does foreclosure move in Nevada?
sections.html:
Most Nevada foreclosures run through a power of sale in a deed of trust under NRS 107.080, and the process has a built-in waiting period. After a notice of default and election to sell is recorded, the trustee cannot sell until at least 3 months have passed, and the statute separately requires that the borrower has failed to cure the default for 35 days.

The notice of sale has its own steps. The trustee must give notice by mail, post a notice for 20 days in a public place in the county, and publish it once a week for three consecutive weeks in a newspaper of general circulation. Those steps give an owner a visible calendar.

An owner who knows a notice of default has been recorded still controls the sale until the trustee's sale. Selling before that date can pay the loan off from proceeds. Ask the lender or trustee for a payoff statement in writing, and read the notice itself for dates, because this summary does not replace it.

sections.h2: What are the probate size tiers?
sections.html:
Nevada sorts estates by value, and the tier decides how fast a house can be sold. NRS 146.080 allows a transfer by affidavit after 40 days only when the decedent left no real property in Nevada, and the limit is $150,000 for a surviving spouse and $25,000 for any other claimant.

A court can set aside an estate of $150,000 or less without administration under NRS 146.070, and a summary administration is available when the gross value after encumbrances does not exceed $500,000 under NRS 145.040. Above that, regular administration applies. The probate page on this site covers the steps in detail.

sections.h2: Where do homestead and landlord rules fit?
sections.html:
Nevada's homestead statute shields up to $605,000 of equity from forced sale on a creditor's judgment, and the exemption does not stop a tax sale or a mortgage foreclosure. Our homestead page walks through a declaration, recording and what happens when the home is sold.

For rentals, NRS 118A sets a security deposit cap of three months' periodic rent, a 60 day written notice for a rent increase, and a rule that a tenant keeps the lease when the house is sold. NRS chapter 40 sets the notice periods for removing a tenant through the courts. Our landlord and tenant page explains how those fit with a sale.

faqs.q: How many counties does Nevada have?
faqs.a: Nevada has 16 counties and one independent city, Carson City. Clark County, which includes the Las Vegas area, had a Census Bureau population estimate of 2,407,226 on July 1, 2025, and Washoe County had 509,386.

faqs.q: When are Nevada property taxes due?
faqs.a: Taxpayers who pay in four installments owe them on the third Monday of August, the first Monday of October, the first Monday of January and the first Monday of March under NRS 361.483. Your county assessor or treasurer bills the tax and can give an exact balance.

faqs.q: What is the Nevada real property transfer tax?
faqs.a: It is $1.95 for every $500 of value in all counties, with an extra $0.10 in Washoe and Churchill Counties and an extra $0.60 in Clark County, according to the Nevada Department of Taxation. The county recorder collects it when the deed is recorded, along with a Declaration of Value.

faqs.q: Does a Nevada seller have to give the buyer a disclosure form?
faqs.a: Usually yes. NRS 113.130 requires the seller to complete the form and serve it at least 10 days before conveyance, with exceptions such as foreclosure sales and sales by a fiduciary who holds title only to arrange a sale for a deceased or incapacitated person.

faqs.q: How long does a Nevada trustee's sale take?
faqs.a: The statute requires at least 3 months after the notice of default is recorded and a 35 day cure period, then notice of sale by mail, 20 days of posting and three weekly publications. The actual date depends on the notice, so read the recorded documents.

faqs.q: Where can I find the guide for my city or county?
faqs.a: Use the city and county links on this page. Each local guide covers the assessor, treasurer and recorder for that place, and the statewide guides explain the rules that apply everywhere in Nevada.
